About.title: About Trillion
About.slogan: An eye for stocks — for everyone.
About.sub: Every lens, as data — the judgment is yours.
About.problemBody: Investment information is scattered, and the market is loud with predictions and tips. Chat rooms sell you "the stock that will go up"; paid tools hide their method inside a black box. In between, individuals end up leaning on what someone else says. The problem is not too little information — it is the lack of a tool to read it with your own eyes. When someone sells you a stock with great confidence, the first thing to look at is not the confidence — it is their incentive.
About.lensTitle: The TR-AI Lens — how we read a stock
About.lensIntro: We read one stock through several published methods, each on its own. Every lens answers just one honest question, and writes down — right on the screen — which metrics it uses and whose research it leans on.

lens.momentum: Momentum — is the trend continuing? (trend persistence)
lens.value: Value — is it cheap against earnings and assets? (the Graham philosophy · the value premium documented by Basu 1977 and Fama-French HML)
lens.quality: Quality — how well does it turn assets into profit? (Novy-Marx 2013 · gross profits ÷ assets)
lens.fscore: F-Score — is the balance sheet weak? (Piotroski 2000 · a 9-point financial-health checklist)
lens.lowvol: Low Volatility — steady per unit of risk? (the low-volatility anomaly)
lens.extra: Asset Growth · Technical — over-investment and overheating signals. (RSI — Wilder 1978 · moving averages)

About.lensClose: Nothing is hidden. Not a black box — a lens we open. Each lens shows the numbers behind it, and when the data is not there, that lens simply says "insufficient data." Reference-grade lenses, though, are weighted the same as verified ones when we tally the overall read.
About.noRecTitle: We do not predict, and we do not recommend
About.noRecBody: There is no "buy this stock" signal here. A lens hands you evidence, not certainty; material, not a conclusion. We set several viewpoints side by side — the decision to buy or sell is entirely yours. A good tool does not make the call for you. It only helps you make a better one.
About.coverageBody: {markets} — {count} markets. For each, we take first-hand material — prices, news, filings — from public sources and show it as it is. We do not invent values. And when the data looks odd, we do not erase it on a hunch.
About.step1: Pick a stock, read the lenses. See at a glance how one stock reads through momentum, value, quality, financial health, and more — each on its own.
About.step2: Read the disagreement. When the lenses disagree is the most important signal — cheap but weak, or pricey but sturdy?
About.step3: You make the call. The material is gathered; the conclusion is yours. We do not press the button for you.
About.quote: “The best thing a human being can do is to help another human being know more.”
About.disclaimer: Trillion does not trade, broker, or advise on financial products, and does not intermediate any transaction. The information Trillion provides is for reference only and is not a solicitation or advice to invest.

EtfLens.etnBody: This product is an ETN (exchange-traded note). The issuing brokerage contracts to pay the return of an underlying index, so it is a strategy product and, unlike an ETF, it has no individual holdings (basket). The product name carries the issuer, the tracked index, and the type (leveraged or inverse).
EtfLens.etnWarn: ⚠️ An ETN carries the credit risk of its issuer.
EtfLens.etnWarnLeveraged: Leveraged and inverse types track a multiple of, or the opposite of, the underlying index, so their value can erode when held for a long time (volatility decay).

RevDcfMethod.title: Reverse-DCF methodology
RevDcfMethod.intro: This metric decodes the expectations already priced into the stock. It does not set a fair value — it surfaces the growth period the market demands and leaves the judgment to you.
RevDcfMethod.structure: The source is Rappaport & Mauboussin, Expectations Investing. We use its calculation structure but source the inputs ourselves from SEC filings and Damodaran public data. So the accurate phrase is not “source-grade” but “source structure + our sourcing.”
RevDcfMethod.repro: Running the Domino Pizza example from the source through our engine gives $285.2 per share / 8 years (source PIE table: $285.20 / 8 years). Using the WACC worksheet (T7) figures as-is gives 7 years instead — the result is sensitive enough to a single rounding digit that it swings by a year. The engine reproduces; differences come from how inputs are sourced.
RevDcfMethod.verificationCaveat: The reproduction above matches a single case the source itself published. There is no contemporaneous outside source to check the per-stock results we compute today against, so whether these figures are correct has never been externally verified.
RevDcfMethod.ledgerTitle: How we differ from the source (disclosed as-is)

growth.w: No consensus data — historical, not an analyst forecast

tax.w: The source itself also uses a firm-specific cash tax rate in the cost-of-capital calculation — the method is not different, only the vintage of the value is. That input, the cash tax rate, is not reliably available for most names and carries anomalies, so we substitute the marginal rate instead. For reference, the effective tax rate Damodaran reports for the broad U.S. market excluding financials averages {taxEffMoney}% for profitable firms and {taxEffAgg}% in aggregate — both lower than the {taxMarginal}% marginal rate we use.

wc.w: Marginal varies 40%p year to year. Subtracting all current liabilities produces a different sign than the source method for some stocks. Within what we have checked, that difference has not changed a verdict. Damodaran cautions that working capital should not be assumed to keep getting more negative forever — at some point the change must flatten or reverse. As of today, {wcPct}% of our {wcTotal} computable results carry a negative working-capital rate.

cap.o: Marginal (adopted the source method as of 880)
cap.w: Reproduces the Domino source anchor at 11.6% (880) — measured six alternatives and adopted the only one that connects to the source. Cost: computable for 90.3% (9.7% not computable), 101 negative values, 133 extreme values (|x|>1) — disclosed, not softened

wacc.s: Company-specific funding rate and beta (Domino: vendor beta of 1, actual bond yield)
wacc.o: Assembled from an industry-average credit spread plus an industry unlevered beta, relevered
wacc.w: Domino source: 5.354% (2020) vs ours: 7.19% (2026) — most of the gap is timing (risk-free rate 0.65% to 3.95%), not method. How far the industry approximation drifts from an individual company has not yet been measured

term.w: The terminal formula (NOPAT×(1+i)÷(WACC−i)) is identical to the source — the value used for i differs by vintage: a 2020 snapshot in the source (1.6%) versus our current expected inflation (Damodaran DB)

sensitivity.s: User adjusts it in the spreadsheet
sensitivity.o: We compute and show a 3-point band
sensitivity.w: Fully automated across names, so the user cannot change inputs; the GAP is most sensitive to the cost of capital (cost of capital ≫ growth ≈ margin)

distribution.w: A benefit of computing every name daily

RevDcfMethod.betaCaveat: The cost of capital is computed with CAPM. Research finds beta explains little of the cross-section of stock returns (Fama-French 1992). Since the GAP is sensitive to the cost of capital, we show a range rather than a single number.
RevDcfMethod.universeCaveat: Trillion calculates its reverse DCF only for companies listed on US exchanges (NYSE, Nasdaq, and others). 486 over-the-counter (OTC) names (as of 2026-08-02) fall outside this scope — of those, we could obtain a market value for 133, and only 8 actually produced a number of years. The reason we leave them out is price: this model works backward from the share price to infer what the market expects, and OTC quotes are not real-time and trade infrequently, which makes that starting point unreliable. There is another view — Professor Damodaran, whose industry and tax-rate data we rely on, includes OTC names precisely to avoid sampling bias. We know that view and chose differently, which is why we disclose, in numbers, exactly how much we do not see.
RevDcfMethod.notInvestmentAdvice: This is neither a forecast nor a recommendation. It is material to judge for yourself.
